agenda.say:
Good morning, and welcome to Case Management. Before a single lesson, a quick game: two truths and a lie, Case Manager edition. I say three things about the job, you vote with your hands.

One: a Case Manager can tell a client what their case is worth. Two: if it isn't in the CMS, it didn't happen. Three: the Conflict Check comes before the matter is even opened. {name}, which one's the lie? Number one, and by lunch you'll know exactly why.

Here's how today runs. First the lessons: John Doe's case, then your role, the line between sharing facts and giving legal advice, reading the raw file, the Case Plan and his treatment, then the car side of things, the do's and don'ts, the repair, the rental.

Then the Practice Lab, seven Skill Activities on his real file, including the firm's backup drive. Then the Knowledge Check.

By the end of today his matter is open the right way, and his car problem has a plan. Now the teaser. Somewhere on John Doe's file there's a damaged car, and nobody has worked out yet whose it is.

That one detail decides who gets a rental. I'm keeping the answer until this afternoon. And a confession: my first week, I thought CMS stood for Can't Miss Saturday. It doesn't, but you'll still never miss a deadline in it.
agenda.ask: {name}, of everything on today's agenda, which part do you think a brand-new Case Manager gets wrong most often?

lab.say:
Quick show of hands: who's ever built flat-pack furniture without reading the instructions? Hands up if there were screws left over. {name}, I see you.

This is the Practice Lab, and today there are no leftover screws. Open the tools on this slide now, the CMS first, beside the slides.

We'll run seven Skill Activities on John Doe's real file, in order. First, you open his case in the CMS, with the Conflict Check before anything else. Second, you link your Google Drive and build the firm's backup folders.

Third, a voicemail: the other side's adjuster wants to record John's story. You plan it and deliver his Direction Packet. Fourth, you assign those directions in the system. Fifth, the Civic investigation: whose rental is it, really?

Now, you could click around until the screen turns green. Please don't. I want every field matching a document, every correction with its source, every step logged.

Why so fussy? Months from now an adjuster reads this file, and what you type today is page one of the story they believe.

{name}, you're my CMS navigator. {name}, you're my fact checker. Stuck on one step for more than ten minutes? Log what you have and move on; we'll fix it in the debrief.

And one little mystery: a helpful colleague has already left a mistake waiting for you in activity one.
lab.ask: {name}, before you click anything, which document will you keep open beside the CMS, and why that one?

wrap.say:
Okay, before the Knowledge Check, let's step back. Quick game first: finish this sentence, one breath each. On a brand-new file, the one thing I will never do is… {name}, go. {name}, you're next. Love it.

Now the real question for the room. Robert Smith's insurance company has already called John Doe, and he needs a car to get to work. What do you tell him today, in what order, and what has to be on the file before tomorrow's claim set-up?

The easy answer is "don't talk to them, we'll handle it, bye." What I actually want is the do's and don'ts in plain words, the rental path laid out, every step logged the same day, and anything legal routed to Atty. Thorne.

I once had a client who, trying to be helpful, told the other side's adjuster his whole life story, including the part about his old football knee. That knee showed up in every offer for a year.

What John says this week lives in the adjuster's notes for the life of the case. So, two or three answers, each tied to a moment on his file from today.

Then your mystery for tonight: tomorrow we send the letters that tell every insurance company we represent him. How many companies is that, and which one would John never have guessed is involved?
wrap.ask: {name}, what's the very first thing you'd tell John Doe, and why that first?

agenda.say:
Welcome back, everyone. Let's settle last night's mysteries before we even sit down.

Quick game: guess the number. Somewhere on John Doe's file there's a number of days that changes everything. Shout your guesses. {name}? {name}?

It's fourteen. Fourteen days between the crash and his first real visit to a doctor, and today you'll see why an adjuster circles that in red.

Second mystery: how many insurance companies get our letters today? Three. The other driver's insurer for the bodily injury claim, the insurer on the car he was riding in, and one he'd never have guessed, a policy he's covered by through his family.

That's the stack, forty thousand dollars of coverage, and we'll prove every layer in writing.

So here's today. Claim set-up first: the stack, the letters of representation, which are just the letters that say talk to us, not our client, and the Case Plan to Atty. Thorne.

Then treatment: keeping John reachable, getting every bill paid by the right payer, and keeping his care moving when life gets in the way. Then a big Practice Lab and the Knowledge Check.

One teaser. Before we're done, one of today's insurance companies is going to try to get John on a recorded call. Some Case Managers only find out afterward. You'll see it coming.
agenda.ask: {name}, of the three insurance companies, which one do you think will be the hardest to pin down in writing?

lab.say:
Practice Lab time, and honestly, today it's a marathon, so stretch. Ten Skill Activities on John Doe's file.

Would you rather chase one adjuster for a week, or three for one day? {name}? Good news: today you get both.

Open the CMS first and keep it beside the slides. You'll build and verify his Policy Stack, send the letters to all three insurers, audit the Coverage Matrix, which is our one-page map of who covers what, flag the fourteen-day gap, and route the Case Plan.

Then the treatment side: outreach when John goes quiet, the warning letter, and the letters of protection that let a clinic treat now and get paid from the settlement.

After that, the Health Plan's payback right, the A-C-T crisis steps when his care gets disrupted, and a referral he won't attend. Then the backup drive: records and bills kept apart.

Same rhythm every time: Your Case, Your Task, Check Your Work.

Here's the thing about notes. "Called client" tells nobody anything. Who, when, which channel, what was said and what happens next: that's a note. Every one of those becomes proof we did our job when the adjuster says we didn't.

{name}, you're tracking our time. Stuck ten minutes? Log it and move on.

Mystery for you: if one of today's letters went to the wrong address, which one would cost John the most money?
lab.ask: {name}, which of today's activities do you think protects the most money down the road?

wrap.say:
Before the Knowledge Check, let's step back. Quick lightning round: one word for today. {name}? {name}? I heard "paperwork" twice, and honestly, I'll allow it.

Now the real question. It's 04/08/2026. Keystone confirmed its limit in writing on 03/20, Riverton Spine & Rehab reports John Doe has missed two visits, and Dana Whitfield has asked John for a Recorded Statement. What do you do first, second and third, and what does each one protect?

"Call John back sometime this week" won't cut it. Shut the recorded call down through the firm the same day, reach John on every approved channel and log it, and get the missed visits to Atty. Thorne with the facts and a plan.

I once had a client who skipped therapy because the clinic's parking lot "had bad vibes." Turned out the bus had stopped running. So ask why before you assume.

Each missed visit is a gap the adjuster will quote back to us, which means every step today protects the settlement. Let's take two or three answers and tie each to a moment on his file from today.

Then tonight's mystery: tomorrow, John explains his fourteen-day gap on a recorded call with you. What's the one question you must never ask him?
wrap.ask: {name}, which of those three moves would you make first, and what does it protect?

agenda.say:
Good morning! Let's close yesterday's mystery first: what could we have done the day John's ride ended? {name}? Yes: asked the clinic about transportation help, logged it, and told Atty. Thorne that same day.

And the one question you never ask him about the gap? The one that hands him an answer, like "it was because of work, right?" His facts, his words. Hang on to that, because today the file gets judged.

Warm-up game: hot or cold. I name something, you shout hot if it helps a demand, cold if it hurts. A dated doctor's note. Hot. An unexplained gap. Cold. A client who told the adjuster he's fine. Ice cold. {name}, you're scorekeeper.

Here's today. First, John explains his fourteen-day gap on a recorded call with you, facts only, no legal advice.

Then the pre-demand audit: every bill checked against the records, and the Specials, which are just his out-of-pocket damages like Medical Bills, totaled to the cent.

Then a strategy session with Atty. Thorne, and the demand itself: a Time-Limited Demand, which is an offer with a deadline. Then the negotiation, and the Net Sheets that show where every dollar goes.

A pile of paper isn't a demand. A story with proof on every page is.

Teaser: by this afternoon we'll have a number with a comma in it, and a puzzle about where it all goes.
agenda.ask: {name}, what's one thing that would make you nervous about putting a deadline on our own demand?

lab.say:
Practice Lab. Fourteen Skill Activities, and three of them talk back.

Quick show of hands: who's ever practiced a hard conversation in the shower first? {name}, very confident, I like it.

Today you'll practice on AI versions of the real people: John Doe on his gap, Atty. Thorne in the strategy session, and the adjuster in the negotiation.

Open the CMS first. You'll build the Gap Explanation Record from John's own words, audit the Specials, and audit the backup drive against the CMS.

Then you'll serve the bodily injury demand with its deadline, and quality-check the two UM demands behind it. UM is the coverage that pays when the other driver's insurance runs out.

Then you negotiate, close the forty thousand, and build both Net Sheets, the page that shows the client every dollar in and out. Same rhythm: Your Case, Your Task, Check Your Work.

Please don't just read the script back to the AI. Listen, take notes, and ask the next question. A sloppy number in the demand can give the insurer an excuse to say it never had a fair chance.

{name}, you're on the calculator. {name}, you check their math. Stuck ten minutes? Log it and move on.

Mystery: one figure on the Net Sheet is one you'd never read to John. Spot it.
lab.ask: {name}, when the AI adjuster brings up the gap, what's your first move?

wrap.say:
Before the Knowledge Check, let's step back. Quick game: rate today's stress level on the adjuster's hold-music scale, one to five. {name}? {name}? Fair enough.

Now the real question. It's 07/20/2026. The Specials are audited and Atty. Thorne has approved a policy-limits demand to Keystone. What must be true before the Time-Limited Demand goes out, and what would let Keystone say it never had a fair chance to settle?

"Send it and hope" is not a plan. Every record and bill included, every number matching the audit, the deadline clear and reasonable, proof it was received, and Atty. Thorne's sign-off on all of it.

I once watched a demand go out with a page of someone else's case stapled in the middle. The adjuster sent it back with a sticky smile and a lot less urgency.

One missing page can turn a strong demand into an argument about fairness, and that argument costs the client time and money. Let's take two or three answers and tie each to something you did today.

Then tonight's mystery: we collected forty thousand gross. Tomorrow, the bills come for their share. How much do you think ends up in John's pocket, and who decides how it gets split?
wrap.ask: {name}, what one thing would you check twice before the demand leaves the building?

agenda.say:
Good morning. Last night I asked how much of the forty thousand ends up in John's pocket. So let's play price is right: closest guess without going over wins. {name}? {name}?

Write your numbers down. I'll reveal the real one this afternoon, to the penny.

And who decides the split? Not us. Atty. Thorne and the client do, from the numbers we prove.

Here's today. First the money side of Track A, the file that settled. We audit the release, which is the paper John signs to end the claim, so it doesn't accidentally let anyone else off the hook.

Then the liens, the bills that get paid out of the settlement, and the provider balances: we ask for reductions, in writing, with reasons. Then the final Net Sheet and the disbursement, meaning the money actually goes out.

Then Track B, the version where the case doesn't settle. Mediation, where a neutral person helps both sides talk, and arbitration, where a neutral person decides. Hard dates, the UPL line at hearings, and two binders built tab by tab.

Some Case Managers take the first lien number and move on. Not you. You ask, you document, and you ask again, because every dollar saved goes to the client.

Teaser: there's one sentence in Keystone's release that could cost John far more than any lien. Find it.
agenda.ask: {name}, before we start, what's your guess: which bill on John's file will be the hardest to reduce?

lab.say:
Practice Lab. Thirteen Skill Activities, two sides of the same file.

Quick game first: true or false? A lien holder will always reduce a bill if you ask nicely. {name}? False. You need reasons, records and math. Asking nicely just gets you a nice no.

Open the CMS first. On the settled side, you'll run the Health Plan and statutory lien reductions, negotiate provider balances, and finish the final Net Sheet with both tabs.

Then you audit the release, trigger the disbursement, and back up the lien file, once you find a missing folder.

On the unsettled side, you'll route the UM impasse to arbitration or court, audit the court's hard rules and set the calendar cutoffs, and calendar the mediation and the arbitration with every date that hangs off them.

Then you map the ADR rules and the UPL line, and build both binders. Same rhythm: Your Case, Your Task, Check Your Work.

Everything printed in any order isn't a binder. I want six tabs where the attorney finds any page in ten seconds. Why care? The mediator reads the first few pages and forms an opinion before lunch.

{name}, you're our calendar captain. {name}, you're checking the math to the penny. Stuck ten minutes? Log it and move on.

Challenge: check every date against its source letter. A date that doesn't add up never gets on our calendar.
lab.ask: {name}, which number on the Net Sheet will John look at first, and how will you explain it?

wrap.say:
Before the Knowledge Check, let's step back. Quick reveal first: John's net is $20,359.92. {name}, how close was your guess? Nearest without going over gets bragging rights and first pick of the good pen.

Now the real question. Keystone's draft release arrives on 08/14/2026 releasing “all other persons, firms, corporations and insurers.” Harbor Point hasn't answered the consent request, and Atty. Thorne is out of the office until Monday. What do you do, and what must not happen before he's back?

It's tempting to say it's just a form and send it to John to sign. Don't. Flag that language, because it could release the UM insurers too. Chase Harbor Point's consent in writing, log everything, and make sure nothing gets signed until Atty. Thorne reviews it.

I once saw a client sign a release in a parking lot because he was so excited to be done. It took months to fix.

That one sentence could cost John the rest of his recovery, so it waits for the attorney. Let's take two or three answers and tie each to something on today's file.

Then tonight's mystery: tomorrow is the litigation fork. Pick one document from your binders. Would it hold up in front of a judge, or only a mediator?
wrap.ask: {name}, what's the one thing that must not happen before Atty. Thorne is back, and why?

agenda.say:
Good morning, and welcome to our last day. Last night's question: would your binder document hold up in front of a judge? {name}? {name}?

The honest answer for most of you: only if we can prove where it came from and that nobody changed it. And that's today.

Quick game: TV or real? I describe a courtroom moment, you tell me if it happens on TV or in real life. A surprise witness bursts through the doors. TV. A deadline missed by one day costs the case. Real.

A lawyer yells objection and the whole room gasps. Mostly TV. A Case Manager catches a missing exhibit the night before. Very real, and that's you.

Here's today. The litigation fork, where a file stops negotiating and goes to court, and moving it there without losing a deadline. Then the court work: filing, service, which just means officially delivering the papers, discovery logs, trial prep, and the car dispute.

Then John's deposition, which is his sworn interview, the defense saying he was partly at fault, and a client who disappears. Then the arbitration award, the final backup audit, and closing a case we drop.

Good Case Managers don't wait for the attorney to ask. It's already on the calendar.

Teaser: at some point today, John changes his phone number. Guess why that matters.
agenda.ask: {name}, of everything on today's list, which part are you most nervous about, and why?

lab.say:
Practice Lab, the last and biggest one: sixteen Skill Activities.

Quick would-you-rather: would you rather e-file at four in the afternoon or at 11:59 at night? {name}? Correct answer: four. Always four.

Open the CMS first. You'll trigger the litigation fork and move the file to litigation status, e-file the complaint and calendar service, fire the CMS countermeasures when work gets stuck, and clear a bottleneck. Then the logs: pleadings and discovery, and the trial-prep checklist.

Then the car: Repair Estimates against what the car was worth, Loss of Use, and Diminished Value, the drop in a car's value just because it's been in a crash.

Then John's deposition prep and a mock cross-examination, the comparative liability package, and skip-tracing a client who's vanished.

And to finish, the Litigation Net Sheet for the award, the final backup audit that gets John's file ready to close, and closing a Dropped Case. Same rhythm: Your Case, Your Task, Check Your Work.

Doing the task isn't enough today. Do the task and calendar everything it starts. In litigation, a missed date isn't an awkward email, it can end the claim.

{name}, you're our deadline hawk. {name}, you're verifying every exhibit. Stuck ten minutes? Log it and move on.

Challenge: for every deadline you set today, name the date it counts from and the document that proves it.
lab.ask: {name}, when a deadline depends on another date, which one do you calendar first, and why?

wrap.say:
Before the last Knowledge Check, let's step back one more time. Quick game: one sentence, what will you do differently on your first real file because of this week? {name}? {name}? Hold onto those.

Now the real question. It's 01/05/2027. Opposing counsel's paralegal says your client's discovery responses are late, John Doe has changed his phone number, and the deposition is set for 02/18/2027. What do you do today, in what order, and what's Atty. Thorne's call, not yours?

"Email John and wait" isn't going to save this one. Confirm the real discovery deadline on the calendar, tell Atty. Thorne today, start the outreach on every approved channel and log it, and if John stays silent, begin the skip-trace steps, all while protecting the deposition date.

Whether to ask for more time, or what to tell the other side, is Atty. Thorne's call.

I once found a client who'd changed his number because he "needed a fresh start." His new voicemail was full by Tuesday.

Late discovery can cost the client evidence and money, so today matters. Let's take two or three answers and tie each one to something from this week.

Then your last mystery: on your first real file, which of these three problems shows up first?
wrap.ask: {name}, of those three problems, which one would you tackle first, and why?
